module_title: Logistics and Distribution from Cold Room

lessons.title: Order Picking and Staging in Cold Environment
lessons.body: When you pick orders in a cold room, speed and accuracy protect both the meat and your fingers. Start by putting on your freezer gear: insulated gloves, a bump cap, and a freezer suit rated for -25Â°C. Grab a picking list that shows order number, customer name, product type (beef, goat, chicken), cut, weight, and destination. In a typical 410-beast cold room, you might pick 20 orders per shift. Use a pallet jack or a roll cage trolley to move between racks. Always pick from the oldest stock first (FIFO). Check the label: each box or carcass tag has a kill date and batch number. If you see ice crystals inside the vacuum bag or a dull grey colour, set it aside for quality check. Do not mix species on the same pallet unless the order says so. For small orders, use a hand-held scanner to confirm barcode. If no scanner, write the batch number on the picking slip. Work in 20-minute bursts, then warm your hands for 2 minutes in the anteroom. Staging means moving picked orders to a designated cold staging area kept at -18Â°C or colder. Never leave meat on the dock at ambient temperature. Stack boxes so air can circulate: leave 5 cm gaps between pallets. Use pallet covers if the staging area is near a door. Label each pallet with a large tag showing order number, destination, and pick time. If you have a blast freezer, stage there only if the order will ship within 2 hours. Otherwise, keep in the main cold room. At the end of picking, count your picks against the list. Report any shortages or damaged goods to the supervisor immediately. A single mistake can mean a rejected shipment and a lost customer. So double-check weights: a 410-beast cold room might handle 200 kg of beef per order. Use a platform scale rated to 300 kg. Record actual weight on the picking slip. Finally, clean your trolley and area with a food-safe sanitizer before the next shift.

lessons.title: Loading Dock Procedures and Temperature Control
lessons.body: The loading dock is the weakest link in the cold chain. Your job is to keep the cold air in and the hot air out. Before loading, check the dock seal: rubber bumpers and curtains must be intact. If the trailer is not sealed against the dock, cold air escapes and meat warms up. Use a dock shelter or inflatable seal if available. Set the dock leveller to match the trailer height. Turn on the dock light and check the trailer interior: it must be clean, dry, and pre-cooled to -18Â°C or colder. If the trailer is warm, do not load. Use a calibrated infrared thermometer to check the trailer wall temperature. Load pallets quickly: aim for 10 minutes per pallet. Use a forklift or pallet jack. Stack heavy boxes at the bottom, lighter on top. Never block the trailer's air return vents. Leave 10 cm between pallets and the trailer ceiling. For a 410-beast cold room, a typical shipment is 1,000 kg of frozen beef. That fits in a 20-foot container. While loading, keep the dock door closed as much as possible. Use strip curtains or a rapid roll door. Check product temperature with a probe thermometer: insert into the thickest part of the meat. It must be -18Â°C or colder. If it reads -15Â°C, reject the pallet and return to cold room. After loading, close the trailer doors and start the Transport Refrigeration Unit (TRU). Set the TRU to -20Â°C for frozen meat. Record the time you started the TRU. Seal the trailer with a numbered bolt seal. Write the seal number on the Bill of Lading. Finally, clean the dock with a broom and sanitizer. Remove any meat scraps. Pests love warm docks. If you see condensation on the floor, mop it up. A wet dock is a slip hazard and a bacteria risk. Always wear steel-toe boots and high-visibility vest. Never stand behind a reversing trailer.

lessons.title: Transport Refrigeration Unit (TRU) Checks
lessons.body: A Transport Refrigeration Unit (TRU) is the engine that keeps meat frozen on the road. Before every trip, do a 10-point check. First, look at the TRU unit: it sits on the front of the trailer. Check for diesel leaks, loose belts, and damaged hoses. Second, start the TRU and listen for unusual noise. A squealing belt means it needs tightening. Third, check the fuel level: the TRU has its own diesel tank. Fill it to at least 75% before a long trip. Fourth, set the temperature: for frozen beef, set -20Â°C. For chilled goat, set 0Â°C to 2Â°C. Fifth, check the defrost cycle: the TRU should defrost every 4 to 6 hours. If it doesn't, ice builds on the evaporator coil and cooling stops. Sixth, inspect the evaporator coil for dirt and frost. Clean with a soft brush. Seventh, check the condenser coil: it must be free of dust and insects. Eighth, test the high-pressure switch and low-pressure switch. Use a manifold gauge set if you have one. Ninth, check the door switches: when the trailer door opens, the TRU should stop or go to low speed. If not, adjust the switch. Tenth, record the TRU hours and any fault codes. Common fault codes: 101 (high pressure), 102 (low pressure), 103 (sensor failure). Write these in the TRU logbook. During the trip, check the TRU every 4 hours. Look at the temperature display: it should stay within 2Â°C of setpoint. If the temperature rises above -15Â°C for frozen meat, call your supervisor. Never turn off the TRU to save fuel. A spoiled load costs 10 times more than diesel. In Africa, dusty roads clog condenser coils quickly. So carry a spare air filter and a brush. If the TRU fails, use dry ice: 50 kg of dry ice per 1,000 kg of meat will hold for 24 hours. But dry ice is expensive. Better to maintain the TRU. Always keep a spare belt and fuel filter in the truck.

lessons.title: Cold Chain Documentation for Shipments
lessons.body: Paperwork is your proof that the meat stayed cold. Without it, a customer can reject a whole truckload. Start with the Bill of Lading (BOL). It must show: shipper name, consignee name, date, trailer number, seal number, product description, weight, and number of pallets. For a 410-beast cold room, a typical BOL lists 1,000 kg of frozen beef, 20 pallets, and a seal number like SA123456. Next, the temperature log. Use a data logger that records every 5 minutes. Place one logger in the trailer near the door and one in the middle of the load. After the trip, download the data. Print a graph showing temperature stayed between -20Â°C and -18Â°C. If any spike above -15Â°C, write an explanation. Third, the cold chain certificate. This is a one-page form signed by the loader and driver. It states: pre-cool temperature, loading time, TRU setpoint, and any deviations. Fourth, the veterinary health certificate. For export, you need this from the government vet. It confirms the meat is from a registered abattoir and disease-free. Fifth, the halal certificate if required. Keep all documents in a plastic folder inside the truck cab. Never leave them on the dock. At delivery, the receiver checks the seal number against the BOL. If the seal is broken, the receiver must note it on the BOL and take photos. Then check the temperature log. If the log shows a break, the receiver can reject the load. So always keep the TRU running. After delivery, scan or photograph all documents and email them to the office. Keep hard copies for 6 months. In many African countries, customs officers ask for the cold chain certificate. If you cannot show it, they hold the truck for days. That costs money and warms the meat. So train every driver to carry and protect the documents.

lessons.title: Returns and Recalls Management
lessons.body: Sometimes a customer returns meat. Maybe the temperature rose, or the cut was wrong. You must handle returns fast to protect other stock. First, park the returning truck away from the cold room door. Do not open the trailer until you have a plan. Put on your freezer gear. Check the seal: if broken, take photos. Then use a probe thermometer to check the meat temperature. If it is -18Â°C or colder, you can accept it for re-inspection. If warmer than -15Â°C, reject it. Do not bring warm meat into your cold room. Second, segregate the returned meat in a quarantine area at -20Â°C. Label it 'RETURN - DO NOT SHIP'. Third, inspect each box. Look for ice crystals, off-smell, or discolouration. If any doubt, condemn it. For a 410-beast cold room, a return might be 200 kg. You can re-freeze only if the meat stayed below -18Â°C the whole time. If it thawed, send to rendering or pet food. Fourth, complete a Return Authorization (RA) form. Note: customer name, reason, batch number, weight, and temperature at receipt. Fifth, investigate the cause. Was the TRU faulty? Did the driver leave the door open? Fix the root cause. Sixth, recalls. A recall happens when you discover a safety problem, like Listeria. You must act within 24 hours. Use your batch records to find every customer who received that batch. Call them. Send a recall notice by email and SMS. Ask them to stop selling and return the product. Document every call and message. Keep a recall log. In Africa, many small shops do not have email. So call the owner directly. If you cannot reach them, visit the shop. Seventh, after recall, destroy the meat under veterinary supervision. Get a destruction certificate. Finally, review your HACCP plan. Add a new control point if needed. Train staff on the new procedure. A recall can cost thousands of dollars, but a food poisoning death costs lives and your business. So act fast and honestly.

lessons.title: Coordination with Distribution Centers
lessons.body: A distribution center (DC) is a hub where you send large shipments, and they break them into smaller orders for shops. To work well with a DC, you need clear communication and standard rules. First, agree on a delivery schedule. For a 410-beast cold room, you might send a full truck to the DC every Monday and Thursday. The DC needs to know the exact arrival time so they can prepare a dock. Second, share your temperature log and cold chain certificate before the truck leaves. The DC will check them at arrival. If the log shows a break, they will reject the load. Third, use a standard pallet size: 1.2 m x 1.0 m. Stack boxes so the DC can scan barcodes easily. Put one label on each box and one master label on the pallet. The master label shows: product, batch, weight, and destination store. Fourth, the DC will have its own cold rooms at -18Â°C. Your truck must back up to their dock seal. If their dock is warm, ask them to pre-cool. Fifth, do a joint temperature check at handover. Use your probe and their probe. Write both readings on the transfer form. Sixth, agree on a return policy for pallets and crates. Most DCs charge a deposit. Get your deposit back by returning clean pallets within 7 days. Seventh, use electronic data interchange (EDI) if possible. But in many African settings, a simple WhatsApp message with a photo of the BOL works. Eighth, train your drivers to be polite and patient. DC staff are busy. A driver who argues can cause a 2-hour delay. Ninth, review performance monthly. Track: on-time delivery, temperature compliance, and rejected loads. Aim for 98% on-time and zero temperature breaks. Tenth, visit the DC regularly. Walk their cold room. Check if they store your meat correctly. If you see boxes on the floor or near the door, speak to the manager. Your brand depends on how they treat your product. So build a partnership, not just a transaction.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Logistics and Distribution from Cold Room

In a 410-beast cold room operation, the product leaving your door is only as valuable as the temperature it holds on the way to the buyer. For African agribusinesses â whether you are supplying butcheries in Nairobi, hotels in Accra, or export consolidators in Durban â the distribution leg is where margin is won or lost. A carcass that leaves at â18 Â°C and arrives at â8 Â°C is a rejected consignment, a spoiled relationship, and a sunk cost. This practical reference covers the six core disciplines of cold room logistics: order picking and staging, loading dock procedures, transport refrigeration unit (TRU) checks, cold chain documentation, returns and recalls, and coordination with distribution centres. Each section is written for operators who need to move product profitably, not just safely.

1. Order Picking and Staging in Cold Environment

Picking in a â18 Â°C room is a productivity and safety challenge. Operatives can safely work in cold storage for limited periods; the UK Health and Safety Executive recommends limiting continuous exposure at â18 Â°C to around 20 minutes, with warmed break areas between picks. In practice, African cold rooms often run longer shifts because labour is cheaper than automation. The business cost is twofold: reduced pick accuracy and higher staff turnover from cold stress.

Use batch picking by destination. If you are supplying three butcheries in one Nairobi suburb, pick all three orders in one pass. This reduces door openings â the single largest driver of temperature loss. Stage picked pallets in a chilled anteroom (0 Â°C to 4 Â°C) rather than the main freezer. The anteroom acts as a buffer: it protects the frozen product, gives you a place to label and manifest, and keeps the main cold room door closed.

Label every pallet with destination, product code, weight, and pick time. In African markets where multiple distributors may share a truck, mislabelling is the most common cause of rejected deliveries. A simple colour-coded tag system (red for export, blue for domestic wholesale, green for retail) costs almost nothing and prevents costly mix-ups.

Table 1: Cold room picking performance benchmarks
Metric Target African context note
Pick rate (cases/hour) 80â120 Lower if manual handling; higher with pallet jacks
Pick accuracy â¥ 99.5% Colour-coded tags reduce errors
Staging time (dock to truck) â¤ 20 minutes Critical at 35 Â°C+ ambient
Door openings per shift â¤ 15 Batch picking reduces this by 40%

Source: Compiled from GCCA (2020), Global Cold Chain Alliance operational benchmarks, and FAO (2019) cold chain guidelines.

2. Loading Dock Procedures and Temperature Control

The loading dock is the weakest link in any cold chain. In most African facilities, the dock is open-air or partially covered. When outside air is 38 Â°C and the truck body is â18 Â°C, every second the door is open is a thermal assault. The solution is not expensive: a dock shelter or curtain strip system can reduce heat ingress by 70% at a fraction of the cost of a full refrigerated dock.

Pre-cool the truck before loading. A TRU should run for 30â45 minutes before the first pallet goes in. If the truck has been sitting in the sun, the walls themselves are heat reservoirs. Loading a warm truck is like putting ice in a hot thermos â the product pays the price.

Use a loading sequence that minimises door-open time: load the furthest pallets first, keep the dock door closed between pallet movements, and use a dock seal if available. For smaller operations, a simple plastic strip curtain costs under $200 and pays for itself in one rejected load avoided.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Ammonia and COâ Refrigerant Exposure

Cold rooms and TRUs in African facilities frequently use ammonia (R717) or carbon dioxide (R744) as refrigerants. Ammonia is toxic and flammable at high concentrations; COâ can cause rapid asphyxiation in confined spaces. Never enter a machine room or cold room after a refrigerant alarm without self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) and a trained buddy. Ensure gas detection sensors are calibrated quarterly and that all staff know the emergency shutdown procedure. In 2021, a refrigerant leak at a cold storage facility in Lagos hospitalised four workers â all because the alarm was ignored. Safety is not a cost; it is the licence to operate.

3. Transport Refrigeration Unit (TRU) Checks

A TRU is a diesel-powered or electric refrigeration system mounted on the trailer. In Africa, diesel TRUs dominate because grid power is unreliable. Before every trip, the driver or loading supervisor must complete a TRU check. This is not optional â it is the difference between a delivered load and a dumped one.

Check the following: fuel level (enough for the full trip plus 25% reserve), refrigerant sight glass (no bubbles), belt tension, battery charge, and the set point. Record the set point and actual box temperature. If the TRU cannot hold â18 Â°C in 40 Â°C ambient, it is not fit for export. Many African exporters have learned this the hard way at the port.

For long-haul routes â Nairobi to Mombasa, Accra to Kumasi, Durban to Johannesburg â use a TRU with a data logger. The logger creates an auditable temperature record that buyers increasingly demand. If a dispute arises, the logger data is your defence.

Table 2: TRU pre-trip checklist and acceptable ranges
Check item Acceptable range Action if out of range
Fuel level â¥ 75% of tank Refuel before departure
Box temperature (pre-cool) â18 Â°C Â± 2 Â°C Run TRU until reached; do not load
Refrigerant sight glass Clear, no bubbles Call technician; do not depart
Belt tension 10â15 mm deflection Adjust or replace
Data logger Recording, time-stamped Replace or reset before loading
Door seals No gaps, pliable Replace seals

Source: Adapted from Thermo King and Carrier Transicold service manuals, and FAO (2019) Food and Agriculture Organization cold chain guidance.

4. Cold Chain Documentation for Shipments

Documentation is where African cold chain operators often lose money. A shipment without a temperature record, a health certificate, or a delivery note is a shipment that can be rejected without recourse. The documentation pack for a frozen meat consignment should include: commercial invoice, packing list, health certificate from the veterinary authority, temperature logger data, delivery note with receiver signature, and â for export â a certificate of origin.

In the East African Community and ECOWAS regions, border officials increasingly require electronic pre-clearance. Kenya's Single Window System and Nigeria's e-Form M are examples. If your documentation is incomplete, your truck sits at the border while the clock ticks on your cold chain. Build a documentation checklist into your loading process. The person who loads the truck should not release it until the paperwork is verified.

5. Returns and Recalls Management

Returns happen. A buyer rejects a load because the temperature spiked, or because the product does not meet specification. A recall happens when a safety issue is identified. Both require a documented process. In Africa, where regulatory oversight varies, your own recall procedure is your reputation insurance.

For returns: quarantine the product immediately in a separate area. Do not put it back into saleable stock until it has been inspected and, if necessary, re-tested. For recalls: identify the batch, notify all recipients within 24 hours, and document the recall in writing. The cost of a recall is high, but the cost of a food safety incident â in lives and in brand damage â is far higher.

6. Coordination with Distribution Centres

Distribution centres (DCs) are the handover point. In Africa, DCs range from modern facilities in Johannesburg and Nairobi to informal consolidation points in smaller towns. The principle is the same: agree on the handover protocol before the truck arrives. Who checks the temperature? Who signs the delivery note? What is the acceptable temperature range? What happens if the DC's cold room is full?

Send an advance shipping notice (ASN) by WhatsApp or email with the truck registration, expected arrival time, product list, and temperature set point. This simple step reduces waiting time â and waiting time in a 35 Â°C yard is cold chain loss. Build relationships with DC managers. In African agribusiness, trust is the most effective logistics technology.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Batch pick by destination â reduce door openings and staging time.
  • Pre-cool the truck â 30â45 minutes before loading, verify â18 Â°C.
  • Keep dock doors closed â use strip curtains or shelters; every second counts.
  • Complete TRU check â fuel, belts, refrigerant, data logger, door seals.
  • Verify documentation pack â invoice, health cert, logger data, delivery note.
  • Record temperatures at pick, load, and delivery â no record, no defence.
  • Quarantine returns immediately â never mix with saleable stock.
  • Send ASN to DC â truck reg, ETA, product list, set point.

Further Reading

  • FAO (2019) â Cold Chain Management for Perishable Foods (free PDF, Food and Agriculture Organization)
  • Global Cold Chain Alliance â Resources and Best Practices (free guides and benchmarks)
  • Thermo King Service Manuals (free TRU maintenance documentation)
  • Carrier Transicold Africa â Service Support (regional TRU support and manuals)
  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (free food safety guidance applicable to cold chain)

This module is part of the Rise AFRICA Skills programme. Course: Cold Room for 410 Beasts. For training enquiries, contact your regional agribusiness hub.

quiz.q: What is the first thing you should do before picking orders in a cold room?
quiz.explanation: Freezer gear protects you from frostbite and hypothermia.

quiz.q: Which stock should you pick first?
quiz.explanation: FIFO (First In, First Out) ensures older meat is shipped before it spoils.

quiz.q: What temperature should the cold staging area be kept at?
quiz.explanation: Frozen meat must stay at -18Â°C or colder to prevent bacterial growth.

quiz.q: How often should you warm your hands when picking in a cold room?
quiz.explanation: Short breaks prevent numbness and loss of dexterity.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see ice crystals inside a vacuum bag?
options: B) Set it aside for quality check
quiz.explanation: Ice crystals indicate temperature abuse or freezer burn.

quiz.q: What is the maximum time meat should be left on the dock at ambient temperature?
quiz.explanation: Meat warms quickly; 10 minutes is the safe limit for staging.

quiz.q: What should you check before loading a trailer?
quiz.explanation: A warm trailer will thaw the meat during transport.

quiz.q: How long should loading one pallet take?
quiz.explanation: Fast loading minimizes cold air loss from the trailer.

quiz.q: What is the minimum temperature for frozen meat at loading?
quiz.explanation: Frozen meat must be at -18Â°C or colder to be safe.

quiz.q: What should you do with a pallet that reads -15Â°C?
options: B) Reject and return to cold room
C) Put it in the sun
D) Ship it with dry ice
quiz.explanation: -15Â°C is too warm for frozen meat; it must be re-chilled.

quiz.q: What is the first step of a TRU pre-trip check?
quiz.explanation: Leaks can cause fire or engine failure.

quiz.q: What temperature should you set the TRU for frozen beef?
quiz.explanation: -20Â°C provides a safety margin for frozen meat.

quiz.q: How often should the TRU defrost?
quiz.explanation: Regular defrost prevents ice buildup on the evaporator coil.

quiz.q: What does fault code 101 mean on a TRU?
quiz.explanation: Code 101 indicates high refrigerant pressure, often due to a dirty condenser.

quiz.q: How often should you check the TRU during a trip?
quiz.explanation: Regular checks catch temperature rises early.

quiz.q: What should you do if the TRU fails and you have no dry ice?
quiz.explanation: The supervisor can arrange a replacement TRU or dry ice.

quiz.q: What document shows the seal number and product weight?
quiz.explanation: The Bill of Lading is the primary shipping document.

quiz.q: How often should a data logger record temperature?
quiz.explanation: Frequent recording provides a detailed temperature history.

quiz.q: What should you do if the seal is broken at delivery?
options: B) Note on BOL and take photos
quiz.explanation: A broken seal may indicate tampering or temperature abuse.

quiz.q: How long should you keep hard copies of cold chain documents?
quiz.explanation: 6 months covers most regulatory and customer audit periods.

quiz.q: Where should returned meat be placed?
quiz.explanation: Quarantine prevents contamination of good stock.

quiz.q: What temperature must returned meat be to accept it?
quiz.explanation: Only meat that stayed frozen can be re-inspected.

quiz.q: What form documents a return?
quiz.explanation: The RA form tracks the reason and condition of returned goods.

quiz.q: How quickly must you act on a recall?
quiz.explanation: Fast action prevents illness and further distribution.

quiz.q: What should you do with recalled meat?
quiz.explanation: Destruction prevents unsafe meat from re-entering the food chain.

quiz.q: What is the standard pallet size for distribution?
quiz.explanation: Standard pallets fit most forklifts and truck widths.

quiz.q: What should a master label on a pallet show?
quiz.explanation: This information helps the DC route the pallet correctly.

quiz.q: How often should you review performance with a DC?
quiz.explanation: Monthly reviews catch problems early and improve service.

quiz.q: What is the target for on-time delivery?
quiz.explanation: High on-time delivery keeps customers satisfied and reduces costs.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see DC staff storing your meat near the door?
quiz.explanation: The manager can correct the storage to protect quality.
